newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boissonnat urges Franco-German awareness on euro.
newsitem.headline: Boissonnat urges Franco-German awareness on euro.

text.p: Bank of France monetary policy council member Jean Boissonnat said on Sunday that greater Franco-German understanding was needed over how to manage a future single European currency.
Without referring directly to government positions or plans for a stability pact, Boissonnat wrote in a newspaper that debates over the issue "are going on and they are real."
"French and Germans need to agree -- between themselves and with their partners -- on how to manage the future euro," he said in an article in Sunday newspaper Journal du Dimanche.
"The French need to understand that the Germans are giving up the mark, which has been very successful for them, without being sure about the stability of the euro," he said.

"And the Germans need to understand French people who do not want rigid and automatic sanctions to manage the new currency without taking into account countries' individual situations at any particular moment."
It was a question of both sides trying to do more to understand the mentality of the other, he wrote.
Boissonnat's remarks appeared in a front-page article given over mainly to drubbing calls for a devaluation of the franc led by former French president Valery Giscaard d'Estaing last week.

Analysts have said France seems at odds with Germany over a planned budget stability pact meant to ensure that countries which join a single European currency, the euro, in 1999 do not then go on to run up big budget deficits.

While Germany is insisting on a numerical definition of the exceptional circumstances which could exempt countries from paying fines under the pact, French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said this month it would be very unwise to fix a figure.
Germany's apparent insistence on getting its own way on the pact has been taken badly in some political circles in France and some politicians have nicknamed it an "austerity pact."

France and Germany put on a united front on Thursday by issuing a joint statement repeating their commitment to European monetary union and, in response to devaluation calls, saying the current franc-mark rate reflected economic fundamentals.
